text:
Keep the Join: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone declares that joined-up handwriting is finished. The reasoning sounds sensible. Children will spend their adult lives typing, tapping and dictating. Lessons on looping a "k" into an "e" look like a leftover from the inkwell era, as useful as teaching them to sharpen a quill. Finland stopped requiring cursive in 2016. In 2010 the Common Core standards in the United States left it out, and many American schools dropped it. Surely, the argument goes, the hours spent on joining letters could go on coding, oracy, or more reading.

I think that argument is wrong. Primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting. They should teach a plain, fluent, practical join rather than ornamental copperplate, and they should teach it well. Handwriting is not nostalgia. It is a tool children think with, and joined handwriting is the form of that tool that works best at speed. Abandoning it would save little time and cost a good deal.

The first thing to understand is that handwriting in primary school is not mainly about presentation. Nobody wants seven-year-olds to master joining because neat pages look nice on parents' evening. They need it because writing by hand is one of the main ways young children learn to compose. A child writing a story is juggling several demanding tasks at once: holding an idea in mind, finding the words, spelling them, remembering punctuation, and physically forming the letters. Working memory in a young child is small. Every bit of attention that goes on how to make a letter is attention taken away from what to say.

That is why handwriting fluency matters so much, and why researchers who study children's writing keep returning to it. Studies by Virginia Berninger and colleagues in the United States, among others, have repeatedly found that the speed and automaticity of letter formation predicts the length and quality of what children write, especially in the early years. When the handwriting is effortful, composition suffers. When it becomes automatic, the mind is freed to think about content. The goal of handwriting teaching, then, is to get children to the point where they no longer have to think about it.

This is where joining comes in. A well-taught joined style is, for most children, faster and more fluent than printing once it is established. In unjoined print, the pen leaves the paper after every letter and has to find its way to the start of the next one. Each lift is a small decision and a small delay. A joined hand turns a word into a single movement, or a few movements, that the hand can learn as a unit. Over time, common letter strings such as "ing", "th" and "ed" become motor patterns of their own. This is the same thing that happens when a pianist stops reading individual notes and starts playing phrases. Joining is not decoration added on top of handwriting. It is how handwriting becomes fast enough to keep up with thought.

There is also a good case that joined writing supports spelling. When the hand learns a word as one flowing movement, the sequence of letters is stored in a second way, alongside its sound and its look. Many teachers report that children who join fluently "feel" when a word is wrong. The research here is less settled than the evidence on fluency, and I would not claim more than it supports. But it fits with what we know about how motor memory and language interact, and it costs nothing extra: children who learn to join are practising spelling patterns every time they write.

The strongest objection to all this is technological. Why spend any effort on handwriting when children will type? The answer is that typing does not replace handwriting at primary age, and there are reasons to think it should not.

First, the practical point. Most of a primary child's writing is still done by hand, and much of their schooling will be too. In England, for example, many public exams are still handwritten. A teenager sitting a two-hour history exam needs to write quickly and legibly for a long time without their hand seizing up. Children who never learned an efficient joined hand often develop slow, cramped printing that collapses under time pressure. By then it is late to fix.

Second, there is growing evidence that the physical act of writing letters helps children learn them. Karin James and her colleagues at Indiana University found that pre-school children who practised printing letters by hand showed more adult-like brain activity when later looking at letters than children who had typed or traced them. Other studies have pointed in a similar direction, including EEG work by Audrey van der Meer and colleagues in Norway suggesting that handwriting engages brain networks linked to learning more than typing does. None of this research is the last word, and some of it concerns handwriting in general rather than joining in particular. But it should make us cautious about assuming that the keyboard is a neutral substitute. Producing a letter shape with your own hand seems to teach you what that letter is in a way that pressing a key does not.

Third, there is the matter of note-taking and thinking. Much has been made of a 2014 study by Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer suggesting that students who took lecture notes by hand understood the material better than those who typed, because handwriting forced them to summarise rather than transcribe. Later attempts to replicate the finding have produced mixed results, so it would be wrong to lean on it too hard. But the underlying idea is plausible: writing by hand is slower than typing, and that slowness pushes the writer to choose and condense. That is a useful habit, and it depends on being able to write by hand quickly enough that the effort is in the choosing, not in the letter formation. Again, a joined hand is what gets most people there.

The objection about time also deserves an honest answer. Yes, teaching joined writing takes curriculum time, mostly in Years 1 to 4. But we should be clear about the alternative. Schools that abandon joining do not stop teaching handwriting. They still teach print, and children still need practice to become fluent. The extra cost of teaching joins on top of correctly formed print is modest, especially if letters are taught from the start with the "exit flicks" that make later joining natural. The cost of not doing so falls later, on older children who write slowly, and on secondary teachers who find they cannot read the work.

A more serious objection concerns children who find handwriting hard, including some with dyslexia, dyspraxia or developmental coordination disorder. For these children, the argument goes, insisting on a joined hand adds a needless hurdle. I take this seriously, and the answer is not to insist rigidly on joining for every child. Some children will do better with print, or with early access to a keyboard, and good schools already make these adjustments. But it is worth noting that many specialists in dyslexia have long recommended joined writing, precisely because it reduces the number of decisions about where letters start and helps prevent common reversals such as "b" and "d". The existence of children who need a different approach is an argument for flexibility, not for dropping joined writing for everyone. We do not stop teaching reading because some children struggle with it.

Another objection is that joined handwriting is old-fashioned and exclusive, a matter of copperplate loops and a fussy insistence on neatness that once marked out the well-schooled from everyone else. Here critics have a point about the past. Some handwriting teaching has been more about obedience and appearance than about function, and children were marked down for untidy work in ways that had little to do with learning. But the cure for bad teaching is better teaching. The joined styles used in most English primary schools today are not ornamental. They are simple, legible, and designed for speed. If anything, removing joined handwriting would make the problem of exclusion worse. Children from homes where adults write by hand, and who get extra practice outside school, will still learn to write fluently. Children who rely on school for the skill will not.

Finally, there is a reason for teaching joined-up writing that is harder to measure but still real. Handwriting is one of the few ways children make something entirely their own. A child's hand develops character over time. Being able to write a card, a letter, a list or a note without a device is a small kind of independence, and it will remain useful for life, whatever technology does. Many adults who were never taught to join say they regret it, and that their handwriting feels childish and slow. That is not a trivial loss, and it is one schools can easily prevent.

None of this means that primary schools should ignore keyboards. Children should learn to type properly, and touch-typing deserves a better place in the curriculum than it usually gets. But typing and joined handwriting are not rivals for the same job. Typing is for producing and sharing finished text quickly. Handwriting, at primary age especially, is for learning letters, learning to spell, and learning to compose. The two skills complement each other, and a good school can teach both.

So the question is not whether joined-up handwriting is old. It is whether it still does useful work for children, and it does. It turns handwriting from a slow, effortful process into a fluent one, and that fluency frees young minds to think about what they are writing. It supports letter learning, probably supports spelling, and prepares children for years of handwritten work still ahead of them. Taught flexibly, with sensible adjustments for children who need them, it costs little and gives a great deal. Primary schools should keep the join.
